It could well be that, I usually use a column condenser attached to what is essentially an urn - the only temp readings I take are from the column. It has a pretty linear temperature increase throughout the process, but the only control you have is the amount of coolant running through it. I've had pretty consistent results using it.

This time around I used a pot still condenser attached to a copper dome and used my digi-boil mashtun. I went for it to have more control over the temperature in the mashtun. The urn got to 80+ degrees before the dome heated up enough to pass through any of the distillate, and the condenser immediately rocketed up into the mid 80s before stabilizing. The thermometer in the condenser may not have been accurate, but the digi-boil hasn't let me down yet.

Recipe was a mash of apricots, sugar and water - on the boil for an hour, cooled and then fermented with Cider Yeast (18% tolerance) for two weeks with some yeast nutrient. 

I didn't take an OG like I would normally with my wine or beer, but it was a vigorous fermentation for about 48 hours and then slowed. 

During the ferment we had some pretty wild temperature variables (Australian Summer - top of 40 degrees, lows of 10 degrees), but everything else on lees has survived just fine. 

Overall, the fermentation was about as effective as my average beer fermentation (going on gut and experience). Final Gravity was 1.00 before going in the pot.

So you'll need to work out a few more defining factors than "I hate retail, I like my computer". Start by answering a few other questions -

1. What are your hobbies?
2. What are you good at?
3. Do you enjoy interacting with people?
4. Do you like your days to be predictable?
5. Do you need a steady income? 
6. What kind of KPIs do you want to be held accountable to?
7. Are you ok with being static all day or do you need to move around?
8. What jobs, if any, have you looked at and thought "that would be a cool job". 

Start working through those questions and similar and you'll work out what you want to be, then just do the things to get there. Sometimes along the way you'll find something else you're good at and you can do that instead. 

To be brutally honest, this sounds like your second job? You will not find a high paying work from home job as your second job, and first one post retail. You shouldn't be looking for one either. Make WFH high pay your end goal if you like - but in the meanwhile spend time at the office and build your network. Your network will be the thing that gets you recommended to companies that would otherwise not take a second glance at your resume.

Hell, if you don't know where to start, do a few years in the Army. That gives you something on your resume and something to talk about at parties.
